lesson.title: One Equation, Two Worlds: Euler's Formula and the Phasor Shortcut
lesson.summary: Euler's formula links exponentials to sines and cosines, giving circuit analysis a compact complex exponential notation for the same sinusoids already described by phase angle and angular frequency.
lesson.body:
Euler's formula states that e raised to (j theta) equals cos(theta) plus j sin(theta), where j is the imaginary unit (engineers use j instead of i to avoid confusing it with current). At first glance this looks like a pure mathematics curiosity, an exponential function somehow equaling a combination of cosine and sine, but it becomes one of the most useful tools in AC circuit analysis once you realize what it does: it packages a magnitude and an angle into a single complex number, and that complex number can be manipulated with ordinary exponent and multiplication rules instead of clunky trigonometric identities. Since AC voltages and currents are described by exactly a magnitude and a phase angle, as seen with phase angle and phase shift, Euler's formula gives circuit analysis a direct bridge into complex number arithmetic.

The quantity e raised to (j theta) always has a magnitude of exactly 1, no matter what theta is, because cos squared theta plus sin squared theta equals 1 for every angle. Multiplying a real amplitude Vm by e raised to (j theta) therefore produces a complex number whose magnitude is Vm and whose angle is theta, written compactly as Vm at angle theta in what is called phasor notation. Since a sinusoid v(t) = Vm sin(omega t + theta) is fully described by its amplitude Vm, its angular frequency omega, and its phase angle theta, and omega is shared by every signal in a single frequency AC circuit, engineers can drop the omega t and the time dependence entirely during analysis, working only with the phasor, then reattach sin(omega t + theta) at the end to get back a real time domain answer.

Worked example: consider a phasor voltage of 100 volts at a phase angle of 60 degrees, written V = 100 at angle 60 degrees, or equivalently V = 100 e raised to (j 60 degrees). Using Euler's formula to convert to rectangular form: cos(60 degrees) equals 0.5 exactly, and sin(60 degrees) equals the square root of 3 over 2, approximately 0.8660. So V = 100(0.5) + j(100)(0.8660) = 50 + j86.60 volts. Check the magnitude by reversing the process: magnitude = square root of (50 squared plus 86.60 squared) = square root of (2500 plus 7499.6) = square root of 9999.6, approximately 100.0, confirming the conversion is consistent, since 50 squared is exactly 2500 and 86.60 squared is approximately 7499.56, summing to essentially 9999.56, whose square root rounds to 100.

This rectangular form, a real part plus j times an imaginary part, is what actually gets added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided when analyzing circuits with multiple sources or components, since Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws still apply directly to phasors written this way. Multiplication and division, in turn, are often easier in the polar form, since multiplying two phasors just multiplies their magnitudes and adds their angles. Euler's formula is the exact mathematical hinge that lets you swing between these two representations, rectangular for addition, polar for multiplication, whichever the calculation at hand calls for.

It is worth being explicit that e raised to (j omega t) represents a phasor spinning counterclockwise around the complex plane at angular frequency omega, tracing out the circular motion whose vertical projection is a sine wave. This is the deepest reason omega, the angular frequency introduced earlier, appears baked directly into the exponent: the complex exponential is a rotating version of the sinusoid, with j serving as a ninety degree rotation operator that keeps the real and imaginary parts locked into cosine and sine.
